text: Adenosine (ADO) was selected as a leveling additive for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole. Changes in deposition potential and the generation of new stripping peaks in cyclic voltammetry curves were observed in electrochemical tests of ADO-containing plating solution. The adsorption behavior of ADO on the cobalt surface was investigated using density functional theory calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, and electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Furthermore, the Co 2+ with ADO coordination was simulated via interaction region indicator analysis. Based on the changes of the ADO adsorption sites from the MD and E-FTIR analyses, an intramolecular synergistic acceleration–suppression mechanism was proposed to explain the effects of low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression in cobalt deposition. Surface analysis revealed that ADO exhibited a grain refinement effect, and crystal analysis showed that the Co hcp (002) crystalline plane was preferentially formed. Finally, X-shaped throughhole with a maximum aspect ratio of 2:1 formed cobalt superconformal filling, with a surface deposition thickness of the cobalt layer as low as 1.2 μm and meanwhile a filling rate ≥90 %.

text: Electronic interconnect technology is the key for realizing advanced packaging and chip interconnection. With the development of semiconductor technology, the line resistance of copper considerably increases because of the large mean free path of electrons, copper cannot meet the process requirements of damascene filling. However, cobalt exhibits good electrical conductivity and a small mean free path of electrons [1,2], which can prevent electron scattering at the surface interface [3]. In addition, the coefficient of thermal expansion of cobalt (13.3 × 10^-6/K) is similar to that of silicon (10 × 10^-6/K) [4,5], and the internal stresses generated during high-temperature annealing are smaller than those generated during high-temperature annealing of copper [6]. Cobalt is considered the most promising alternative metal for nanoscale interconnect technology.

text: The bottom-up superfilling phenomenon of cobalt has been increasingly studied, and various micro-nanoscale mechanism models have been proposed. Such models include hydrogen-induced inactivation mechanisms [7,8], voltage-dependent suppression mechanisms [9, 10], S-type negative differential resistance mechanisms [11,12], and differential current efficiency filling mechanisms [13]. Rigsby et al. [12] proposed a differential current efficiency filling mechanism and achieved damascene filling of cobalt. Using the differential current filling mechanism, Ni et al. [14] introduced polyvinylpyrrolidone into electrodeposition of cobalt to achieve a superconformal silicon trench filling. Ma et al. [15,16] used the S-type negative differential resistance mechanism with malachite green and achieved micro blind hole filling of cobalt. Li et al. [17,18] achieved micro blind hole filling with different pore sizes using nitrotetrazolium blue chloride, applicable to S-type negative differential resistance mechanism theory. Huang et al. inves tigated the role of oxime additives and concluded that the amine group can suppress cobalt electrodeposition by coordinating with ${ \bf C o } ^ { 2 + } \ \bar { [ 9 , 1 0 , }$ 19]. In addition, it was proposed that Co $\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) ^ { - }$ was the intermediate for cobalt deposition [20], which explained the difference in cobalt deposition rates at different pH levels. Li et al. [21] delved into the efficacy of 5-alkynylpyrimidines as inhibitors for cobalt superfilling by curbing excessive growth in specific regions to ultimately obtain homogeneous and compact cobalt coating. Ni et al. [22] explored the combined effects of 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate and polyvinylpyrrolidone on the growth dynamics of cobalt pillars during electroplating and uncovered a synergistic interaction to efficiently modulate the morphology and dimensions of these pillars. Cao et al. [23] conducted the effects of dimethylglyoxime, 3-mercapto-2-propanesulfonate, and histidine on the growth characteristics and magnetic properties of cobalt electrodeposited on copper substrates and discovered notable impacts on the coating morphology, structure, and magnetic attributes. Li et al. [24] focused on the electroplating of nanocrystalline cobalt within sulfate baths with butynediol ethoxylate to produce coatings with exceptional crystallinity and superior surface morphology. Tong et al. [25] examined the role of alkyne-PEG4-amine as an inhibitor in cobalt superfilling, showing its superiority in hindering cobalt growth in select areas to achieve even and dense coating. Wu et al. [26] assessed the performance of phenyl methyl sulfoxide as an additive for cobalt superfilling to significantly enhance the coating uniformity and density and improve the reliability of the three-dimensional interconnect. Furthermore, the design of an in-situ micro-reactor electrochemical experiment is crucia for investigating cobalt valence in complex intermediates and tracking its reduction process effects [27].

text: Herein, using adenosine (ADO) as an additive with the lowconcentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression and the differential current efficiency filling mechanism during cobalt deposition, superconformal filling of cobalt in X-shaped through-hole was achieved. Through electrochemical analysis, ADO was observed to exhibit a depolarizing effect on Co ^ 2 + deposition at low concentrations. However, at concentrations of > 1 0 mg/L, ADO increased the polarization of cobalt deposition and considerably changed the cobalt deposi tion. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, this electrochemical effect was elucidated in terms of electrostatic potential (ESP) on the molecular surface and the adsorption energy of ADO on the cobalt surface, respectively. The shift in the type of ADO electrochemical action at different concentrations was elucidated in terms of the change in adsorption sites during electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Finally, cobalt filling with ultrathin surface deposition thickness (SDT) outside the hole was realized via the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect of ADO.

The initial pH of the plating solution was set as ^ 4, but in order to ensure the stable pH of the plating solution during the electroplating process, 0.57 mol /LH_3 BO _ 3 as a buffer was added into the plating solution. At the same time, with the purpose to agitate the solution, air bubbling blow of 2.5 L/min was carried out near the cathode during the plating process. Plating was performed using titanium mesh as an insoluble anode, and a laser-perforated single-layer copper-clad resin plate as a cathode. The surface of the cathode featured dense X - shaped through-hole, the thickness of the resin plate was 160 μm, and the aperture of the through-hole was 80 μm at maximum and 40 μm at minimum. text: The surface ESP of the ADO molecule was within the range from −50.39 to 56.25 kcal/mol, and the higher surface ESP could result in the stronger electrostatic adsorption on the cathode surface [34,35]. The high ESP region of the ADO molecule was extremely dispersed, and the electrostatic adsorption on the cathode surface was in a multipoint adsorption state. The adsorption sites were –NH 2 of adenine moiety and –OH of nucleoside moiety. A lower ΔE suggested that ADO was more likely to receive and provide electrons on the cathode surface during electrochemical reactions while having a larger adsorption strength in the electric field [36–38]. With no MO distribution on the nucleoside group, so it exhibited only electrostatic adsorption and low adsorption strength on the cobalt surface. Thus, the electrochemical active site of ADO was the adenine group. According to the MO distribution characteristics and the electrochemical test results, it was hypothesized that the nucleoside group accelerates cobalt deposition, the adenine group suppresses cobalt deposition, and the adsorption site of the adenine group increased at a high concentration, rendering the suppression effect dominant [39,40]. However, the reliable correlation between simple HUMO-LUMO calculations and inhibition efficiency was questioned in early work [41]. Therefore, more relevant simulations of IRI and MD simulations were added to further support the explanation of ADO suppressesing function during cobalt electrodeposition.

text: To investigate the interaction of ADO with Co ^ 2 + and the complex structure, the distribution of the weak interactions of the complexes was analyzed by the IRI method [42], and the results of the weak interaction visualization analysis were shown in Fig. 3. The strong interactions were masked in the figure to highlight the distribution of the weak interactions. As shown in Fig. 3b, the distribution of the weak interactions of the complexes was near the adenine moiety, and the introduction of Co ^ 2 + resulted in a clear conical interaction zone in the adenine moiety. As shown in Fig. 3c and d, the planar interaction distribution confirmed the enhanced interaction between Co ^ 2 + and adenine moiety, suggesting that the formation of a stable structure between them. The stabilized structure confirmed that cobalt bonded with the adenine group in ADO to generate a complex, which explained the generation of the new electrochemical stripping peaks shown in Fig. 1.

text: DC electroplating was performed to corroborate the effect of ADO on cobalt filling. The through-hole filling of cobalt was conducted in a 1.5 L Haring cell with a current density of 0.5 ~A/dm2 and plated with a DC power supply for 4 h. Cathodic bubbling was employed during the plating process at a bubbling rate of 2.5 L/min. Here, 50 mg/L of ADO was added during plating, and the X-shaped through-hole filling of cobalt was achieved with the SDT value of 1.2 μm. The pH of plating solution was changed nonlinearly during the cobalt deposition because no acidic or basic substances were added to stabilize the pH value. After plating for 1 h, 2 h and 4 h, the pH values of plating solution were observed as 3.2, 2.6 and 2.3, respectively. The rate of cobalt deposition could become slow due to the decrease of pH value [20,59], thereby leading to thin layer of cobalt growth outside the X-shaped through-hole.

text: As shown in Fig. 8a, ADO was adsorbed on the surface of the cathode under electrostatic forces. This resulted in preferential adsorption on the electrode surface outside the pore owing to the difference in liquid mobility and low ADO concentration inside the pore. The DFT calculation, MD simulation, and E-FTIR spectroscopy revealed that the adenine group adsorption increased after the ADO concentration increased, thereby showing suppression of Co ^ 2 + deposition, confirming that ADO accelerated Co deposition at low concentrations and suppressed cobalt deposition at high concentrations during the electrochemical test. Thus, as shown in Fig. 8b, the Co ^ 2 + in the hole was preferentially reduced to Co ^ 0 for accelerating the cobalt deposition, and forming a butterfly-type structure. Although the surface of the electrode outside the hole was strongly suppressed by ADO, the cobalt deposition rate was low and the cobalt layer thickness was below 1 μm. As the deposition process advanced, the curvature of the cobalt layer augmented, leading to an improvement in surface mobility and an increased propensity for ADO adsorption, resulting in a higher adsorption concentration, ultimately suppressing the deposition of cobalt within the pore. As shown in Fig. 8c, the deposition rate decreased. Finally, as shown in Fig. 8d, under the low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression ef fect of ADO, superconformal filling was realized.

text: During the electrochemical test, it was observed that ADO exhibited a low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect. By analyzing the HOMO-LUMO and ESP values, discovered that the ADO adsorption sites could be categorized into two distinct groups: adenine and nucleoside. Subsequent MD simulations revealed that the specific adsorption sites were the –OH within the nucleoside group and the –NH within the adenine group. Furthermore, the E-FTIR test indicated that the –OH in nucleoside group were preferentially adsorbed, and as the concentration of ADO increased, the adsorption of the –NH in adenine group was enhanced. These findings were consistent with the ESP calculations, which identified the –OH in nucleoside group as the maximum point and the –NH in adenine group as the sub-maximum point. Combined with the results of electrochemical tests and IRI sim ulations, it is concluded that the nucleoside groups which containing multiple –OH played an accelerating role in cobalt deposition, while the adenine group which coordinated with Co ^ 2 + played a role in suppressing cobalt deposition.
